terms.grammar: adverb; also an indeclinable noun with a genitive, and with esse, “to be enough”
evidence: Traupman p. 109: sat est, that’ll do
terms.comment: With a genitive, enough of: negōtī satis, enough to do; with esse, “is enough”: semel satis est, once is enough (Cic. Att. 13.52.2). More than enough: satis superque (Catull. 7.2), or plūs satis (Ter. Eun. 85). Lewis & Short: satis is enough so that nothing more is needed, affatim so that nothing more is wanted.

terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica et cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; rarer in prose (Lewis & Short)
evidence: Plaut. Aul. 3.6.24: pol vel legiōnī sat est (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sen. 48: tantum quantum sat est (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: plenty, as much as one wants
evidence: Plaut. Poen. 3.1.31: edās dē aliēnō quantum velīs, ūsque adfatim (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: enough so that one wishes for no more; satis is enough so that one needs no more.

phrases.latin: vēscere, sōdēs. — jam satis est. — at tū, quantum vīs, tolle. — benignē
phrases.english: Do eat, please. — I’ve had enough. — Well, take as much as you like. — No, thank you.

phrases.latin: quaeris, quot mihi bāsiātiōnēs tuae, Lesbia, sint satis superque
phrases.english: you ask, Lesbia, how many of your kisses would be enough and more than enough for me
shut the doors, girls: we have played enough

phrases.latin: aestāte puerī sī valent, satis discunt
phrases.english: in summer, if children are well, they learn enough

phrases.latin: accēde ad ignem hunc; jam calēscēs plūs satis
phrases.english: come to this fire; you’ll soon be more than warm enough
